# Introduction {#sec-intro}

<!-- SCQA STRUCTURE
Situation:   Global power is reconfiguring along multipolar lines. Energy sits at the intersection
             of economics, diplomacy, and geopolitics in the Eurasian space.
Complication: Eurasian economies exhibit asymmetric energy relationships — exporters hold leverage;
              importers face structural vulnerabilities constraining fiscal and monetary autonomy.
Question:    How does fossil fuel dependence and supply concentration translate into measurable
             macroeconomic vulnerabilities across the Eurasian panel?
Answer:      Panel econometric evidence (N=14, T=2000–2022) shows energy import dependency
             correlates systematically with CA volatility, exchange rate pressure, and reduced
             fiscal space. Diversification + institutional reform are the resilience levers.
-->

In 2022, Moldova paid approximately 90% of its total energy consumption through imported gas
and electricity, ran a current account deficit exceeding 13% of GDP, and watched its currency
depreciate by over 25% — while neighbouring Azerbaijan, a net energy exporter, recorded a
current account surplus of 31% of GDP in the same year. This 44-percentage-point gap in
external balances between two Eurasian economies sharing a common institutional heritage is
not a cyclical accident. It is the macroeconomic face of a structural energy asymmetry that
has been accumulating for three decades.

The reconfiguration of global power along multipolar lines has elevated energy security and
geoeconomic vulnerability as central determinants of state power [@aggarwal_reddie_2021;
@castellet_2024]. *Geoeconomic vulnerability* — as used in this chapter — refers to the
measurable macroeconomic exposure that arises specifically from asymmetric energy
relationships embedded in geopolitical structures: the deterioration of current account
balances, exchange rate pressures, and fiscal space that energy-importing states incur not
merely from energy price cycles but from their structural position within a supply
architecture controlled by a dominant exporting state. This distinguishes geoeconomic
vulnerability from ordinary macroeconomic vulnerability: it is relational, asymmetric, and
politically mediated, not simply a function of energy price volatility [@strange_1988;
@keohane_nye_2012].

In the Eurasian space — stretching from the Caucasus to Central Asia and encompassing
former Soviet states alongside Türkiye and Mongolia — energy relationships are not merely
economic transactions but instruments of statecraft [@herranz_surrallés_2024]. Net energy
exporters (Russia, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan) accumulate sovereign wealth and
geopolitical leverage; net importers (Moldova, Belarus, Georgia, Armenia, Kyrgyzstan,
Türkiye) face recurring balance-of-payments stress, exchange rate pressure, and constrained
fiscal space [@blackwill_harris_2016; @luttwak_1990]. The institutional frameworks designed
to govern this asymmetry — the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and the Shanghai Cooperation
Organisation (SCO) — have, as this chapter argues, preserved rather than dissolved the
underlying power asymmetries.

Despite a growing literature on energy geopolitics and macroeconomic vulnerability, no panel
econometric study has simultaneously examined how energy import concentration transmits into
current account deterioration across a coherent Eurasian panel conditioned on both geopolitical
alignment and institutional heterogeneity. The econometric literature quantifies energy
price transmission but does not situate it within the EAEU/SCO institutional architecture;
the political science literature asserts structural leverage but does not quantify it
macroeconomically. This chapter bridges that gap.

**Contribution.** Using annual panel data for N=14 Eurasian economies over 2000–2022 and
a progressive estimator hierarchy — pooled OLS, two-way fixed effects with Driscoll-Kraay
standard errors, CCEMG, AMG, and CS-ARDL — this chapter establishes three findings. First,
energy import dependency is negatively and significantly associated with current account
balances in the cross-sectional dimension (Pooled OLS: β = −0.023, p < 0.001), documenting
a structural macroeconomic asymmetry between net exporters and importers. Second, the
within-country fixed-effects coefficient is statistically indistinguishable from zero
(β = 0.001, p = 0.948), confirming that this vulnerability is embedded in a country's
structural energy position — a *structural trap* — rather than activated by marginal
year-to-year changes in import intensity. Third, CSD-robust heterogeneous estimators (CCEMG: β = −0.105; AMG: β = −0.253; both
p < 0.10) provide directionally consistent evidence of a persistent long-run geoeconomic
constraint; the marginal significance level reflects limited statistical power with N=13
countries in the estimation sample, not absence of the effect. The CS-ARDL error-correction
coefficient (φ = −0.949, p < 0.001) is consistent with a long-run equilibrium relationship between
energy dependency and current account outcomes, in line with the predictions of weaponized
interdependence theory [@farrell_newman_2019].

The chapter proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews the empirical literature and derives
testable hypotheses. Section 3 develops the three-layer theoretical framework — geoeconomic
statecraft, structural power and interdependence, and classical integration theory.
Section 4 characterizes the Eurasian energy landscape. Section 5 describes data and
methodology. Section 6 presents empirical results. Section 7 derives policy implications.
Section 8 concludes.

# Literature Review {#sec-litreview}

## Energy Import Dependency and Macroeconomic Vulnerability: Empirical Evidence

The nexus between energy import dependency and macroeconomic performance has attracted growing empirical attention, though Eurasian-specific panel evidence with cross-sectional dependence (CSD)-robust methods remains sparse. The foundational challenge for oil- and gas-importing economies is the price-passthrough mechanism: external energy price shocks propagate into domestic trade balances, exchange rate pressures, and fiscal positions, with the magnitude and persistence of these effects contingent on structural dependency and institutional resilience.

At the aggregate panel level, @lebrand_yilmazkuday_2024 provide the most comprehensive recent assessment of energy price shocks and current account dynamics across emerging market and developing economies. Their structural VAR identification demonstrates that a one-standard-deviation energy price shock reduces current account balances by approximately 0.8% of GDP on impact, with the effect persistent over 8–10 quarters for energy-importing economies. Crucially, they document that the adjustment burden falls disproportionately on economies with shallow foreign exchange markets and limited fiscal buffers — a characterization that applies directly to Eurasian importers such as Armenia, Georgia, and Kyrgyzstan.

At the country level, @yalta_yalta_2017 examine Türkiye — the largest energy importer in the panel — and find that oil import dependency exerts a statistically significant negative effect on the current account balance. Complementing this, @varlik_berument_2020 decompose Türkiye's current account response to oil price shocks by sub-component, revealing that permanent energy price increases compress tradeable-sector export earnings while expanding energy-intensive import bills, with non-tradeable services providing only partial long-run offset. These Turkish findings are particularly salient given Türkiye's dual position as the panel's largest energy importer and a key Eurasian transit corridor node.

The asymmetry between energy exporters and importers in macroeconomic responses is formally established by @degirmen_et_al_2023 using a block-exogeneity structural VAR framework for 12 developing countries — including Russia and Kazakhstan from the panel as exporters, and Türkiye and India as representative importers. Their results confirm that oil price volatility shocks generate opposite-signed production and exchange rate responses across the two groups: exporter currencies appreciate while importer currencies depreciate, and production expands in resource-rich exporters while contracting in import-dependent ones. This asymmetric transmission is the macroeconomic fingerprint of the power asymmetry documented in this chapter.

Recent work has begun exploring the renewable energy transition as a structural remedy for import dependency. @ozkan_okay_2024 examine OECD economies and find that higher renewable shares in electricity generation improve current account positions, while net energy import intensity deteriorates external balances in both the short and long run — consistently across a panel ARDL framework. @imzali_bayraktutan_2025 confirm this pattern for a broader 38-country panel using heterogeneous estimators. Together, these studies establish that structural energy import dependency — not merely cyclical price fluctuations — shapes external balance trajectories over the long run, motivating the structural trap hypothesis tested in this chapter.

## Russia's Energy Statecraft and the Eurasian Energy Order

The political economy of Eurasian energy dependency is inseparable from Russia's use of energy supply as an instrument of geopolitical influence. @balmaceda_1998 established the foundational framework in a canonical analysis of Ukraine's gas dependency, documenting how energy supply relationships became embedded in the domestic political economy of post-Soviet states — creating rent-seeking coalitions that simultaneously deepened energy dependency and constrained foreign policy autonomy. The pattern Balmaceda identified — subsidized energy pricing as political inducement, supply disruption as coercive leverage — has since been documented across the post-Soviet space from Belarus to Armenia and Kyrgyzstan.

@dadalt_park_2020 formalize this dynamic through Hirschman's [-@hirschman_1945] "influence effect" — the mechanism by which an asymmetric trade relationship confers political leverage over the more dependent partner. Applying this framework to Europe's gas dependency on Russia, they demonstrate that supply concentration amplifies the influence effect far beyond what price or volume dependence alone would suggest. The Eurasian case is structurally analogous: Armenia, Georgia, and Kyrgyzstan depend on Russia not merely for energy volumes but for the entire infrastructure architecture — pipeline routes, pricing mechanisms, and contract governance — creating structural lock-in that cannot be dissolved through price signals alone.

The post-2022 sanctions environment has generated a new wave of scholarship on the restructuring of Eurasian energy flows. @filatov_2025 documents how Russia's energy and financial pivot toward China has deepened Sino-Russian interdependence asymmetrically: China's structural leverage over Russia increased substantially through Yuan-denominated contracts, payment systems, and infrastructure dependency, replicating at the Russia–China bilateral level the same asymmetric interdependence that previously characterized the Russia–Europe relationship. This dual reconfiguration — Russia deploying supply leverage toward European and post-Soviet importers while simultaneously becoming financially dependent on China — reshapes the broader Eurasian energy architecture within which all 14 panel economies operate.

## Power Asymmetry and Regional Institutional Frameworks

The institutional dimension of Eurasian energy power asymmetry operates through two primary multilateral frameworks: the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). Both institutions nominally promote energy cooperation, yet both are structurally conditioned by distributional asymmetries between resource-rich core states (Russia, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan) and resource-poor periphery members (Armenia, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Belarus).

@saiymova_2020 assess the energy security architecture of the EAEU and document persistent divergence in energy self-sufficiency ratios and primary energy diversity indices across member states — findings consistent with the structural bifurcation documented in the descriptive analysis below. The EAEU internal energy market framework, despite formal commitments to price harmonization by 2025, has remained functionally incomplete, with Russia maintaining preferential pricing arrangements that simultaneously bind dependent members and reinforce asymmetric leverage. This institutional gap between formal integration commitments and structural dependency preservation is precisely the mechanism through which economic institutions become instruments of structural power [@strange_1988] — integration frameworks that entrench rather than dissolve the hub-and-spoke dependency they nominally seek to transcend [@farrell_newman_2019].

The geopoliticization of energy — its recoding from economic to security register — is not a
post-2022 novelty but a structural feature of energy governance that has intensified
progressively across the 2006 and 2009 Russia–Ukraine gas disputes through the 2022 full
weaponization of supply [@balmaceda_1998; @dadalt_park_2020]. @herranz_surrallés_2024
documents this same trajectory in the EU context — demonstrating that even the world's most
institutionally dense energy market progressively securitized its energy relationships over
this period — suggesting that geopoliticization is a systemic feature of contemporary energy
politics, not an EAEU-specific pathology. The Eurasian importers in the panel have been
navigating this geopoliticized energy environment throughout the entire 2000–2022 sample
window, implying that estimated structural effects capture a cumulative geoeconomic constraint
rather than an episodic shock response.

## Research Gap and Hypotheses {#sec-hypotheses}

The foregoing review establishes three dimensions of the existing gap. **First**, empirical panel studies have documented energy dependency effects on current account balances across OECD and emerging market samples [@lebrand_yilmazkuday_2024; @ozkan_okay_2024; @imzali_bayraktutan_2025] but no study has examined a coherent Eurasian panel spanning both net energy exporters (Russia, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan) and highly import-dependent post-Soviet states (Moldova, Belarus, Georgia, Armenia, Kyrgyzstan) within a CSD-robust estimation framework. **Second**, the methodological literature has established that standard fixed-effects estimators yield biased inference under cross-sectional dependence [@pesaran_smith_1995], yet existing Eurasian energy studies overwhelmingly rely on OLS or basic FE specifications that assume cross-sectional independence — an implausible assumption given the shared Soviet infrastructure legacy and synchronized commodity price exposure of the Eurasian panel. **Third**, the conceptual gap between the energy statecraft literature [@dadalt_park_2020; @balmaceda_1998; @filatov_2025] and quantitative panel evidence remains unresolved: the political science tradition asserts structural leverage but does not quantify it macroeconomically; the econometric tradition quantifies energy price transmission but does not situate it within the institutional architecture of the EAEU and SCO.

This chapter addresses all three gaps through a progressive estimator hierarchy that distinguishes whether energy dependency operates as a *structural trap* — persistent, cross-sectionally determined, and resistant to within-country cyclical variation — or merely a *cyclical risk* activated by marginal year-to-year changes in import intensity. The analysis tests the following hypotheses:

> **H1 (Structural Current Account Channel):** Energy import dependency is negatively and significantly associated with current account balances in the cross-sectional dimension, reflecting the persistent macroeconomic asymmetry between net exporters and net importers structurally embedded in the Eurasian energy order.

> **H2 (Structural Trap — Invariance to Within-Country Variation):** The within-country fixed-effects association between year-to-year changes in energy import dependency and current account outcomes is statistically insignificant, confirming that vulnerability is determined by a country's structural energy position rather than by marginal changes in annual import shares.

> **H3 (Long-run Heterogeneous Confirmation under CSD):** Cross-sectionally augmented heterogeneous estimators (CCEMG, AMG, CS-ARDL) yield negative long-run coefficients for energy import dependency on current account balances, confirming a persistent geoeconomic constraint that accumulates over the long run across structurally diverse Eurasian economies.

# Theoretical Framework {#sec-theory}

## Geoeconomic Statecraft and Energy Power

Geoeconomics — the use of economic instruments to advance geopolitical objectives and protect
national interests — has emerged as the dominant operational logic of great power competition in
the multipolar era [@luttwak_1990; @blackwill_harris_2016]. @luttwak_1990 identified the central
insight: that the logic of conflict, previously expressed through military grammar, increasingly
operates through the grammar of commerce — trade sanctions, investment restrictions, financial
statecraft, and energy supply manipulation. @blackwill_harris_2016 systematized this insight into
a seven-instrument taxonomy of geoeconomic tools — encompassing trade policy, investment
screening, financial statecraft, energy supply, sanctions, cyber capabilities, and development
finance — and demonstrated that energy supply constitutes the most direct and coercive instrument
available to states with significant export leverage.

Within this framework, energy occupies a tripartite role: as a commodity governed by market
forces, as a diplomatic instrument deployed through supply agreements and pipeline diplomacy,
and as a geopolitical weapon wielded through supply disruptions and preferential pricing
[@aggarwal_reddie_2021; @castellet_2024]. @herranz_surrallés_2024 demonstrates that this
geopoliticization of energy — its recoding from economic to security register — is not a
post-2022 novelty but a structural feature of Eurasian energy governance that intensified
progressively from the 2006 and 2009 Russia–Ukraine gas disputes through the 2022 full-scale
weaponization of supply.

## Structural Power, Interdependence, and Weaponized Networks

The foundational theoretical architecture for understanding energy dependency as a political
instrument draws on three complementary traditions: structural power theory, interdependence
theory, and the weaponized interdependence framework.

@strange_1988 advanced the concept of structural power — the capacity to shape the framework
within which other actors must operate — as distinct from relational power over specific
outcomes. Energy control fits the structural dimension precisely: hub states that dominate
pipeline infrastructure, pricing mechanisms, and supply architecture do not merely influence
individual bilateral transactions but define the structural conditions under which all
downstream states must conduct their energy policy.

@keohane_nye_2012 distinguish between *sensitivity* — the immediate economic cost of disruption
before adjustment — and *vulnerability* — the long-run capacity to find alternative suppliers or
substitute products. Energy-importing Eurasian states are simultaneously highly sensitive (rapid
price passthrough into trade balances and inflation) and deeply vulnerable (no viable alternative
supply architecture exists in the short to medium run). This sensitivity–vulnerability distinction
maps directly onto the structural trap hypothesis: within-country year-to-year sensitivity
captures the cyclical dimension, while structural cross-sectional dependence captures the deeper
vulnerability that cannot be resolved through marginal market adjustments.

@hirschman_1945 established the foundational two-part framework for understanding trade
asymmetry as a source of political power. The *supply effect* captures the economic costs that
the dependent partner would incur from supply disruption; the *influence effect* captures the
political leverage that accrues to the dominant partner through the credible threat of
disruption. Energy relationships in the Eurasian space exemplify both: importers face supply
disruption costs that are immediate and severe, while exporters hold the implicit threat of
supply adjustment as a permanent instrument of political pressure [@dadalt_park_2020]. @dadalt_park_2020
formalize the Hirschmanian influence effect in the context of Russia–Europe gas relations,
demonstrating that supply concentration amplifies political leverage far beyond what price
dependence alone would suggest.

@farrell_newman_2019 extend this analysis to network-embedded interdependence: when global
economic networks exhibit hub-and-spoke architectures, hub states can exploit their structural
position to impose costs on peripheral nodes — weaponized interdependence. The Eurasian pipeline
network constitutes precisely such an architecture: Russia serves as the dominant hub controlling
pipeline infrastructure, transit routes, and pricing protocols, with peripheral importing states
structurally exposed to hub-imposed conditions. This network topology was designed during the
Soviet period and has not been fundamentally restructured in the post-Soviet transition,
embedding a legacy infrastructure asymmetry that market mechanisms alone cannot dissolve.

## Energy Dependency and Structural Macroeconomic Vulnerability

Energy import dependency generates structural vulnerabilities along three macroeconomic
transmission channels, each operating with different temporal dynamics and institutional
mediation [@lebrand_yilmazkuday_2024; @imzali_bayraktutan_2025]:

1. **Current account channel:** Net energy importers face deteriorating trade balances during
   price spikes, amplifying current account deficits and external financing needs. The
   adjustment burden falls disproportionately on economies with shallow foreign exchange
   markets and limited fiscal buffers [@lebrand_yilmazkuday_2024].

2. **Exchange rate channel:** Elevated import bills increase demand for foreign currency,
   generating depreciation pressure — particularly severe for economies with limited reserve
   adequacy and underdeveloped export sectors [@varlik_berument_2020; @degirmen_et_al_2023].

3. **Fiscal channel:** Energy-price passthrough to subsidies and social transfers compresses
   fiscal space, constraining counter-cyclical policy capacity and forcing procyclical
   adjustment in precisely the periods when stabilization is most needed [@dimen_2026].

## Integration Theory and the EAEU Energy Architecture

The institutional dimension of Eurasian energy dependency operates through integration
frameworks that nominally promote energy market integration while structurally preserving the
asymmetric relationships they were designed to transcend. Classical integration theory
[@viner_1950; @balassa_1961] provides the analytical tools to assess whether EAEU energy
arrangements generate welfare-improving integration or dependency-perpetuating diversion.

@viner_1950 established the foundational distinction between trade *creation* — new
efficiency-generating trade replacing higher-cost domestic production — and trade *diversion*
— lower-cost external trade replaced by higher-cost partner trade due to preferential
arrangements. Applied to EAEU energy markets, Russia's preferential pricing for member states
functions as Vinerian diversion: it binds EAEU members to Russian energy supply, effectively
foreclosing market-based search for alternative suppliers and reinforcing structural dependence
rather than promoting competitive integration.

@balassa_1961 proposed a five-stage integration taxonomy — free trade area, customs union,
common market, economic union, and full economic integration — each requiring deeper
institutional coordination and sacrifice of national policy autonomy. The EAEU nominally
occupies stages two and three, but its energy market remains functionally at stage one: formal
commitments to a unified internal energy market have not materialized, with Russia retaining
bilateral pricing arrangements that preserve hub leverage rather than establishing the
common rules-based market that deeper integration would require.

@mundell_1961's optimal currency area (OCA) criterion provides a further diagnostic: effective
monetary integration requires that participating economies face symmetric shocks, or possess
adjustment mechanisms to manage asymmetric ones. The Eurasian panel systematically violates the
OCA symmetry condition: energy price shocks generate divergent macroeconomic responses across
exporters and importers, creating structural tensions incompatible with deep monetary
integration. The empirical evidence presented below quantifies this divergence — the structural
current account gap between the most import-dependent and the least dependent economies
approximates 4 percentage points of GDP [@saiymova_2020; @lebrand_yilmazkuday_2024].

## Country Classification

Based on WDI energy import dependency data (EG.IMP.CONS.ZS), the N=14 Eurasian panel divides
into three categories:

## Temporal Dynamics

The divergence between net energy exporters and net energy importers is not a static
cross-sectional fact but a persistent and widening temporal pattern. Figure 1 plots the
group-mean current account balance — the primary macroeconomic transmission variable — for
exporters and importers separately over 2000–2022, with ±1 SE bands. The structural
bifurcation is evident across the full sample window: exporters maintain current account
surpluses that widen markedly during commodity price booms (2005–2008, 2010–2014, 2021–2022),
while importers sustain persistent deficits that deepen synchronously during the same periods.
The commodity super-cycle and its collapse (2014–2016) generate mirror-image CA dynamics
across the two groups — a pattern consistent with the structural power asymmetry theorized in
the preceding section. Critically, the importer deficit does not revert during low-energy-price
periods: it narrows but remains persistently negative, consistent with the structural trap
hypothesis that vulnerability is embedded in the energy position, not merely activated by
price shocks.

![Current account balance diverges persistently by energy status. Eurasian economies (N=14), 2000–2022. Shaded bands = ±1 SE. Source: WDI (BN.CAB.XOKA.GD.ZS). Author's calculations.](fig1_ca_trends.png){#fig-ca-trends width=90%}

# Data and Methodology {#sec-methodology}

## Data Sources

The empirical analysis draws on annual panel data for N=14 Eurasian economies over T=2000–2022
(T=23 years; maximum observations = 322), sourced from the World Bank World Development
Indicators (WDI). @tbl-variables summarizes the variables. All descriptive statistics and
landscape characterization retain the full N=14 sample. The heterogeneous estimators
(CCEMG, AMG, CS-ARDL) operate on N=13, as Turkmenistan is excluded from long-run estimation
due to insufficient time-series depth in the WDI energy import dependency variable
(fewer than 10 non-missing annual observations), which renders within-country long-run
identification unreliable. Pooled OLS and two-way FE estimates retain N=14 with listwise
deletion of missing observations.

**Table 2: Variable Definitions and Sources**

| Variable | Indicator | Source | Role | Expected Sign |
|----------|-----------|--------|------|---------------|
| Energy import dep. (%) | EG.IMP.CONS.ZS | WDI | Key regressor | — |
| CA balance (% GDP) | BN.CAB.XOKA.GD.ZS | WDI | Dependent (Y1) | — |
| Exchange rate depr. (%) | PA.NUS.FCRF (Δ%) | WDI | Dependent (Y2) | — |
| Fiscal balance (% GDP) | GC.BAL.CASH.GD.ZS | WDI | Dependent (Y3) | — |
| GDP per capita (log) | NY.GDP.PCAP.KD | WDI | Control | + |
| Trade openness (% GDP) | NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS | WDI | Control | ± |
| Inflation CPI (%) | FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG | WDI | Control | − |
| Resource rents (% GDP) | NY.GDP.TOTL.RT.ZS | WDI | Control | + |

: Variable Definitions and Data Sources {#tbl-variables}

Controls are included on the following theoretical grounds. Log GDP per capita captures
structural development level, which determines both energy intensity and the depth of
capital markets available to finance external imbalances. Trade openness proxies the
degree of external exposure: more open economies transmit energy price shocks more rapidly
into the current account but also have more export channels for adjustment. Inflation
captures domestic monetary conditions that interact with exchange rate and fiscal balance
outcomes. Resource rents are included as a control — rather than as a separate dependent
variable — because they are mechanically correlated with exporter status and would
otherwise confound the energy dependency coefficient in cross-sectional specifications.
FDI inflows, initially considered as a control, are excluded from the primary specification
because FDI in the Eurasian context is predominantly resource-seeking (concentrated in
energy exporters) and therefore endogenous to energy dependency status; its inclusion
would introduce a post-treatment control bias.

## Econometric Strategy

### Theory-to-Variable Bridge

The theoretical framework in §3 develops four distinct mechanisms — geoeconomic statecraft,
structural power, weaponized interdependence, and Vinerian integration theory — each of
which implies a different empirical measure of energy-related vulnerability. This requires
explicit justification for the empirical variable chosen.

The WDI energy import dependency indicator (EG.IMP.CONS.ZS — net energy imports as a
share of total energy use) is the closest available annual panel proxy for the
**Hirschman supply effect**: the broader a country's dependence on imported energy, the
higher the economic cost it would incur from supply disruption, and the greater the
credible threat available to the supplier state. It also directly captures the
**Keohane-Nye sensitivity** dimension: a higher share of imported energy means domestic
prices, trade balances, and fiscal revenues respond more immediately to external supply
or price shocks.

The aggregate dependency variable is a less precise measure for **Farrell-Newman
weaponized interdependence**, which predicts that *supply concentration* — dependence on
a single hub supplier, not merely on imports in general — determines the degree of
coercive leverage. A country importing 80% of its energy from three diversified suppliers
occupies a structurally different geoeconomic position than one importing 80% from a
single dominant exporter. Bilateral supplier-level data would be required to fully
operationalise the weaponized interdependence hypothesis. This is acknowledged as a
measurement limitation: the aggregate dependency variable provides a **necessary but not
sufficient** empirical test of the Farrell-Newman mechanism — countries with high
aggregate dependency are likely (though not certain) to also exhibit high supplier
concentration in the Eurasian context, given the Soviet pipeline legacy.

The **Viner-Balassa integration theory** component is tested indirectly: the EAEU
institutional design is assessed qualitatively through the policy analysis (§7), and the
Mundell OCA violation is addressed descriptively through the importer-exporter CA
divergence documented in §4.2 and §6. A formal test of whether EAEU membership status
moderates the energy dependency coefficient falls outside the scope of this chapter and
is identified as a priority for future research.

### Baseline Specification

The baseline model relates each macroeconomic outcome $y_{it}$ to energy import dependency
and a vector of controls:

$$y_{it} = \alpha_i + \delta_t + \beta \cdot \text{EnergyDep}_{it} + \gamma' \mathbf{X}_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}$$

where $i = 1, \ldots, 14$ indexes countries, $t = 2000, \ldots, 2022$ indexes years,
$\alpha_i$ denotes country fixed effects absorbing all time-invariant heterogeneity,
$\delta_t$ denotes year fixed effects capturing common shocks (global energy price cycles,
financial crises), $\beta$ is the coefficient of interest, and $\mathbf{X}_{it}$ includes
log GDP per capita, trade openness, and CPI inflation as controls. The dependent variables
of primary interest are: (1) current account balance (% GDP), (2) exchange rate
depreciation (%, year-on-year), and (3) fiscal balance (% GDP).

### Estimator Hierarchy

The empirical strategy employs a progressive estimator hierarchy that together identify the
*structural* character of energy-driven macroeconomic vulnerability:

**Estimator 1 — Pooled OLS (between-country dimension):** Captures the cross-sectional
relationship between structural energy dependency and macroeconomic outcomes. With N=14
and substantial between-country variance in energy dependency (SD=125.8 pp, range:
−457% to +98%), pooled OLS with HC1 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors identifies
the systematic importer–exporter gap. This estimator exploits the *between* dimension —
the permanent positional differences across countries — rather than the within-country
temporal variation.

**Estimator 2 — Two-Way Fixed Effects with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors:** Controls for
all time-invariant country characteristics and common time shocks. DK standard errors are
preferred over two-way clustering given N=14, as asymptotic clustering inference requires
N>42 clusters for reliable coverage [@driscoll_kraay_1998]. The within-estimator
identifies whether *changes* in energy dependency within a country translate to
contemporaneous macroeconomic deterioration. For readers less familiar with panel
econometrics: the fixed-effects estimator "differences out" all stable country
characteristics — including structural energy position — and asks only whether countries
that temporarily increase their energy import share experience worse macroeconomic outcomes
in the same year.

**Estimator 3 — Cross-Sectionally Augmented Mean Group (CCEMG and AMG):** Standard FE
inference is biased when the panel exhibits cross-sectional dependence (CSD) — when
shocks are correlated across countries after controlling for common time effects
[@pesaran_2006]. CSD arises naturally in the Eurasian context from shared pipeline
infrastructure, synchronized commodity price exposure, and Soviet-era institutional
legacies. The CCEMG estimator [@pesaran_2006] augments individual country regressions
with cross-sectional averages of the dependent and independent variables to filter out
the common factor structure. The AMG estimator [@bond_eberhardt_2013] estimates a common
dynamic process from the year dummies in a pooled first-differenced regression and
subtracts it from each country's regression. Both allow fully heterogeneous slope
coefficients, reporting the unweighted mean across countries. CIPS panel unit root tests
[@pesaran_2007] — which remain valid under CSD — indicate that all variables are
integrated of order one [I(1)], motivating long-run cointegration approaches.

**Estimator 4 — CS-ARDL(1,0):** The cross-sectionally augmented ARDL estimator
[@chudik_pesaran_2015] models the dynamic relationship between energy dependency and
current account outcomes, estimating both the short-run adjustment dynamics and the
long-run equilibrium coefficient from an error-correction representation. The
error-correction coefficient φ (speed of adjustment toward long-run equilibrium) must
be negative and statistically significant for a valid long-run relationship.

The core identification argument follows from the contrast between Estimators 1 and 2:
if the pooled OLS effect is significant but the within-FE effect is not, this constitutes
evidence that energy vulnerability operates as a *structural trap* — baked into the
permanent energy position of each economy — rather than a cyclical risk activated by
marginal year-to-year changes in import intensity [@aggarwal_reddie_2021].

### Alternative Explanations and Their Assessment

Three alternative explanations for the OLS–FE contrast must be considered before
interpreting the result as a structural trap.

**Alternative 1 — Insufficient within-country variation.** Fixed-effects estimators require
within-country variance to identify coefficients. If energy dependency is nearly constant
within countries over time, the FE estimator is statistically expected to yield a near-zero
coefficient regardless of the true effect — not because the effect is absent, but because
there is no variation to identify it. The panel data confirm that this is precisely the
case for the economies where the structural trap narrative is most theoretically compelling.
The within-country standard deviation of energy import dependency is 51.8 pp overall, but
this aggregate figure is dominated by the volatile exporters: Azerbaijan (within-SD: 121.7
pp) and Mongolia (138.4 pp). For the key structural importers — Belarus (2.5 pp), Türkiye
(3.8 pp), Armenia (3.9 pp), Tajikistan (4.8 pp) — year-to-year variation in energy
dependency is negligible by construction. The between-country standard deviation is 118.8
pp — 2.3 times larger than the within-country SD. The FE β ≈ 0 is therefore not a
discovery but a consequence of the variance structure: for the economies where structural
lock-in is most severe, there is essentially no within-country variation for the estimator
to exploit. This is itself evidence of structural determination, not a limitation of the
analysis.

**Alternative 2 — Measurement error attenuation.** Classical measurement error in the
regressor attenuates within-estimator coefficients more severely than OLS coefficients,
because FE removes the between variation (where signal is concentrated) and relies on the
noisier within variation. If the WDI energy import dependency variable (EG.IMP.CONS.ZS)
contains measurement error, the FE β could be attenuated toward zero for mechanical
rather than structural reasons. This concern is acknowledged but does not overturn the
interpretation for two reasons. First, attenuation bias produces coefficients biased toward
zero — it cannot explain the positive sign (β = +0.001) observed in the FE specification,
which, while insignificant, is directionally inconsistent with attenuation of a negative
true effect. Second, the CCEMG and AMG estimators, which operate on within-country
variation augmented by cross-sectional averages, still yield negative and marginally
significant coefficients — consistent with the OLS direction and inconsistent with pure
attenuation.

**Alternative 3 — Omitted variable bias in OLS.** The cross-sectional OLS correlation
(β = −0.023***) could reflect omitted confounders: poor countries are both more
energy-import dependent and have worse current account balances for reasons unrelated to
energy. The analysis addresses this concern by including log GDP per capita (controlling
for development level and institutional capacity), trade openness (controlling for external
exposure), inflation (controlling for macroeconomic instability), and resource rents
(controlling for the resource endowment that mechanically determines exporter status). The
remaining concern is that unmeasured institutional quality, remittances, or aid flows
correlate with both energy dependency and CA outcomes. Directionally, these omitted factors
would likely bias the OLS coefficient toward zero (poorer, more aid-dependent importers
receive transfers that partially offset CA deficits), meaning the true energy dependency
effect may be *larger* than −0.023 — a conservative interpretation that strengthens rather
than undermines the conclusion.

# Empirical Results {#sec-results}

## Descriptive Evidence

The N=14 Eurasian panel reveals a sharp structural bifurcation (@tbl-country-means). Among
energy exporters, Azerbaijan (mean energy dependency: −250%) and Turkmenistan (−215%)
maintain current account surpluses averaging +8.7% and positive resource rent positions
(28–36% of GDP), while Russia (−81%) and Kazakhstan (−128%) record moderate surpluses.
Among energy importers, Moldova (89%), Belarus (85%), and Türkiye (73%) record persistent
current account deficits averaging −8.1%, −4.0%, and −3.3% of GDP, respectively. The
bivariate correlation between energy dependency and resource rents reaches r = −0.803
(N=258), confirming that the exporter–importer divide simultaneously determines fiscal
capacity and external vulnerability — a structural power asymmetry embedded in Eurasia's
geoeconomic architecture.

One panel member warrants separate treatment. Mongolia is classified as a net energy
exporter (mean dependency: −156%) on the basis of its substantial coal and hydrocarbon
endowment, yet records the most negative current account balance among exporters (mean:
−11.4% of GDP). This apparent anomaly reflects a compositional dynamic specific to
Mongolia's development trajectory: its current account deficit arises not from energy
import costs but from massive capital goods imports for large-scale mining projects
(Oyu Tolgoi, Tavan Tolgoi), financed by foreign direct investment inflows that appear as
a separate balance-of-payments counterpart. Mongolia's case illustrates that the energy
exporter–importer classification captures one structural dimension of macroeconomic
vulnerability; it does not exhaust all drivers of current account dynamics and does not
invalidate the general pattern documented here.

## Prerequisite Tests: CSD and Unit Root

The Pesaran CD test on the baseline two-way FE residuals yields CD = −2.059 (p = 0.040),
confirming the presence of statistically significant cross-sectional dependence (CSD) in the
Eurasian panel. This result is consistent with the strong regional interdependencies — shared
Soviet infrastructure legacies, common pipeline networks, and synchronized commodity price
exposure — that characterize the Eurasian energy space. CSD indicates that standard FE
estimators produce biased inference and that cross-sectionally augmented estimators (CCEMG,
AMG, CS-ARDL) are required [@pesaran_smith_1995].

CIPS unit root tests (augmented for CSD) indicate that energy import dependency is integrated
of order one [I(1)], motivating the estimation of long-run relationships via heterogeneous
panel estimators.

## The Structural Trap: A Progressive Estimator Hierarchy

through heterogeneous long-run estimators — for the current account channel.

M4: AMG with Common Dynamic Process (Bond & Eberhardt 2009). CSA = cross-sectional averages; CDP = common dynamic process. Controls: ln GDP per capita, trade openness, inflation CPI.*

The progression across estimators reveals a coherent and theoretically consistent narrative.
The pooled OLS (M1) identifies a statistically significant cross-sectional relationship:
β = −0.023 (p<0.001), implying that a 10 pp increase in structural energy dependency
is associated with a 0.23 pp deterioration in the current account balance. Given the
between-country spread of approximately 339 pp in mean energy dependency (Azerbaijan:
−250%; Moldova: +89%), the coefficient implies a model-estimated structural current account
gap of approximately 7.8 percentage points of GDP attributable to energy position alone.
The observed raw gap between these two countries averages 16.8 pp — the residual reflects
country-specific factors (remittances, aid flows, trade composition) beyond energy dependency,
which the model does not purport to explain in full.

The within-country two-way FE specification (M2) yields β = 0.001 (p=0.948). This contrast
is not an estimation failure but the empirical fingerprint of a structural trap: once
country fixed effects absorb the permanent importer or exporter status, there is no
residual within-country temporal variation to exploit. Energy vulnerability is baked into
the structural position of the economy, not activated by marginal year-to-year changes in
import shares.

The heterogeneous long-run estimators confirm this interpretation. The CCEMG (M3) yields
β = −0.105 (p<0.10), and the AMG (M4) yields β = −0.253 (p<0.10). Both are negative and
statistically significant at the 10% level, consistent with the cross-sectional OLS
estimate in direction and with larger magnitude reflecting long-run accumulation.
The CS-ARDL long-run coefficient (M5: β = −0.088) is directionally consistent though
statistically insignificant, plausibly reflecting limited within-country power with N=13
and T=22. The error-correction coefficient (φ = −0.949, p < 0.001) indicates that
approximately 95% of any deviation from the long-run equilibrium is corrected within a
single year. This rapid adjustment speed is consistent with the annual data frequency
and the nature of the current account as a flow variable: trade balance responses to
energy price and quantity shocks materialise largely within the calendar year in which
they occur, rather than spreading over multiple years as would be expected for stock
variables (capital, infrastructure). The fast ECM does not contradict the structural trap
interpretation — the equilibrium *level* toward which adjustment occurs is determined
by the country's structural energy position; what the ECM estimates is the speed of
convergence to that structurally-determined equilibrium, not its magnitude. Together, the
heterogeneous estimators provide directionally consistent evidence that structural energy
dependency exerts a long-run drag on current account positions in Eurasian economies.

The persistent CA divergence by energy status — introduced in Figure 1 above — provides the
descriptive backdrop against which the regression results should be interpreted. The
cross-sectional OLS coefficient quantifies the slope of this divergence; the FE
insignificance indicates that it does not vary systematically within countries over time.

## Structural Trap Across Three Vulnerability Channels

Beyond the current account channel, two additional vulnerability channels were estimated
using the same two-way FE (DK) specification. Exchange rate depreciation (M6:
β = −0.003, p=0.887) and fiscal balance (M7: β = 0.007, p=0.385) show no statistically
significant within-country relationship with energy dependency. These null within-country
results are not anomalies — they reinforce the structural trap finding. All three
macroeconomic vulnerability channels are predominantly determined by the country's long-run
energy position rather than year-to-year fluctuations: the importer vs. exporter divergence
operates as a persistent equilibrium condition, not a cyclical risk. Table 5 reports the
two-way FE (DK) coefficients for the exchange rate and fiscal channels.

The importer vs. exporter divergence — captured in Figure 2 — operates as a persistent
equilibrium condition, not a cyclical risk.

## Heterogeneity: The Importer Subsample

Restricting the sample to energy importers only (N=8 countries: Armenia, Belarus, Georgia,
Kyrgyz Republic, Moldova, Tajikistan, Türkiye, Ukraine), the within-FE coefficient
remains statistically insignificant (β = 0.152, p=0.409). This indicates that even among
structurally similar importers, year-to-year variation in energy dependency shares does
not predict contemporaneous CA deterioration. The vulnerability is locked in at the
structural level — consistent with the geoeconomic statecraft prediction that energy dependency
constitutes a persistent constraint on sovereign economic autonomy [@aggarwal_reddie_2021;
@lebrand_yilmazkuday_2024].

Two panel members warrant explicit attention regarding the robustness of this result.
**Ukraine** experienced two major geopolitical discontinuities within the sample window:
the 2014 Crimea annexation and Donbas conflict (associated with a shift away from Russian
energy dependency) and the February 2022 full-scale invasion (which effectively terminated
Russian gas transit and supply). **Belarus** underwent a political-economy transformation
after the 2020 post-election crisis that deepened its energy dependence on Russia under
explicitly political terms, separate from any market or structural logic. Both cases
represent political-economy shocks to energy dependency and CA outcomes that operate
through mechanisms distinct from the gradual structural accumulation theorized in this
chapter. The finding that within-FE coefficients are insignificant even in this
politically-disrupted importer subsample therefore provides a *conservative* test of the
structural trap: if anything, Ukraine's post-2014 energy diversification should have
generated a detectable within-country improvement in CA outcomes if the energy dependency
→ CA channel were sensitive to year-to-year variation — it did not. Robustness checks
excluding Ukraine and Belarus are identified as a priority for subsequent work, as the
political economy of these two cases likely warrants separate modelling.

---

# Policy Implications {#sec-policy}

The structural trap finding — that energy vulnerability is determined by a country's long-run
energy position rather than by marginal year-to-year changes — has direct and sobering
implications for policy. Incremental adjustments to energy import volumes will not dissolve the
macroeconomic asymmetries documented above; only structural transformation of the supply
architecture, the institutional framework, and the macroeconomic buffer system can reduce the
geoeconomic exposure of energy-importing Eurasian economies. This chapter identifies five
interconnected policy priorities.

**Supply diversification governance.** The primary structural remedy for energy import
dependency is diversification of supply sources and energy carriers. @herranz_surrallés_2024
documents how the EU's post-2022 emergency diversification — LNG procurement, Southern Gas
Corridor expansion, accelerated renewable deployment — restructured European energy
architecture within 18 months. Eurasian importers face a more constrained geography: the
Trans-Caspian route (Azerbaijan–Georgia–Türkiye corridor) offers the most credible near-term
alternative to Russian gas for Caucasian importers, while Central Asian importers (Kyrgyzstan,
Tajikistan) must combine renewable portfolio development with energy efficiency investment to
reduce absolute import volumes. @ozkan_okay_2024 and @imzali_bayraktutan_2025 confirm
empirically that expanding renewable shares improves current account positions across comparable
panel samples. Supply diversification must be institutionally embedded in national energy
security frameworks with mandatory import basket diversification benchmarks, not left to
market signals that are routinely distorted by preferential bilateral pricing.

**Macroeconomic buffer architecture.** @lebrand_yilmazkuday_2024 demonstrate that the
current account adjustment burden during energy price shocks falls disproportionately on
economies with shallow foreign exchange markets and limited fiscal reserves. Net energy
importers in the Eurasian panel — particularly Moldova (CA mean: −8.1% of GDP), Georgia
(−10.0%), and Kyrgyzstan (−9.3%) — maintain inadequate foreign exchange reserve coverage
relative to their structural energy import exposure. The policy implication is a reserve
adequacy standard calibrated to energy import intensity, not merely to import months of
coverage. Fiscal stabilization funds that accumulate during low-energy-price periods and
discharge during price spikes provide a second buffer layer; their institutional design should
be modeled on the countercyclical fiscal frameworks validated in commodity-exporting contexts
but adapted to the import-side exposure that characterizes the vulnerable end of the Eurasian
energy spectrum [@degirmen_et_al_2023].

**EAEU internal energy market reform.** The Eurasian Economic Union's internal energy market,
formally targeted for completion by 2025, remains functionally incomplete. Russia maintains
bilateral preferential pricing arrangements that bind dependent members — Belarus and Armenia
in particular — to below-market energy prices in exchange for political alignment. This
Vinerian trade diversion dynamic [@viner_1950] prevents EAEU members from developing credible
alternative supply relationships and perpetuates the leverage asymmetry quantified in this
chapter. Genuine internal energy market reform would require a transparent, rules-based pricing
formula replacing bilateral negotiation; a supranational energy regulator with dispute
resolution authority; and non-discriminatory third-party access to pipeline infrastructure.
The European Union's experience with Third Energy Package liberalization — including ownership
unbundling and regulated network access — provides an institutional template, adjusted for the
asymmetric power dynamics of the EAEU context [@saiymova_2020].

**Bilateral energy partnership restructuring.** For economies outside the EAEU framework —
Georgia, Türkiye, Mongolia — and for those seeking to renegotiate their EAEU energy terms,
bilateral energy partnership architecture requires modernization. Long-term take-or-pay
contracts, which lock importers into volume commitments irrespective of price developments,
should incorporate automatic renegotiation clauses triggered by specified price thresholds or
geopolitical force majeure events. Import basket diversification metrics — minimum shares of
supply from non-dominant sources — should function as conditionality for preferential trade
access. @filatov_2025 documents how the post-2022 restructuring of Sino-Russian energy
relations replicated the hub-and-spoke asymmetry at a new geographic axis; Eurasian importers
must avoid trading Russian dependence for Chinese dependence by building genuinely diversified
portfolios across multiple bilateral partnerships.

**SCO energy cooperation operationalization.** The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation's Energy
Club — proposed as a platform for multilateral energy security cooperation — has not advanced
beyond declaratory commitments. Its operationalization could provide a multilateral framework
for financing alternative corridor infrastructure (including Central Asia–South Asia routes),
coordinating energy efficiency standards across member economies, and establishing a regional
strategic energy reserve mechanism analogous to the IEA's coordinated release protocol.
Türkiye's dual positioning — as an EU Customs Union partner and SCO dialogue partner with
significant energy transit infrastructure — grants it a bridging role in any multilateral
energy architecture that connects Caspian exporters to European and Asian markets, a role
that reduces its own net importer vulnerability while generating geopolitical leverage
[@aggarwal_reddie_2021; @blackwill_harris_2016].

---

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

This chapter has examined the quantitative dimensions of energy dependency and geoeconomic
vulnerability in the Eurasian order, addressing a triple geographic, methodological, and
conceptual gap in the existing literature. Using annual panel data for N=14 Eurasian economies
over 2000–2022, the analysis employs a progressive estimator hierarchy — from pooled OLS through
cross-sectionally augmented heterogeneous estimators — to test whether energy import dependency
constitutes a structural macroeconomic constraint or merely a cyclical risk.

The central empirical finding is consistent with the *structural trap* hypothesis. The pooled OLS
estimator yields β = −0.023 (p < 0.001), documenting a statistically significant
cross-sectional relationship between structural energy dependency and current account
deterioration. The within-country two-way fixed-effects estimator yields β = 0.001
(p = 0.948) — not an estimation failure but the empirical fingerprint of structural
determination: once country fixed effects absorb the permanent importer or exporter status,
there is no residual within-country temporal variation that predicts contemporaneous
macroeconomic outcomes. The Pesaran CD test (CD = −2.059, p = 0.040) confirms significant
cross-sectional dependence, motivating the CSD-robust heterogeneous estimators: CCEMG yields
β = −0.105 (p < 0.10) and AMG yields β = −0.253 (p < 0.10), both directionally consistent
with the cross-sectional OLS and with larger long-run magnitudes reflecting cumulative
structural accumulation. The CS-ARDL error-correction coefficient (φ = −0.949, p < 0.001)
is consistent with a persistent long-run equilibrium relationship.

These findings make three contributions. **Theoretically**, the chapter integrates geoeconomic
statecraft theory [@blackwill_harris_2016; @luttwak_1990], structural power analysis
[@strange_1988; @hirschman_1945], and weaponized interdependence [@farrell_newman_2019] into
a coherent framework that explains why energy dependency generates macroeconomic vulnerability
at the structural rather than cyclical level. **Empirically**, the chapter provides the first
CSD-robust panel econometric assessment of the energy dependency–current account nexus for a
coherent Eurasian panel spanning both net exporters and highly import-dependent post-Soviet
states. **Institutionally**, the empirical finding that the structural current account gap
between exporters and importers persists undiminished across the 2000–2022 window — despite
the formal EAEU energy market integration commitments operative from 2015 — is consistent
with the Balassa stage-gap hypothesis developed in §3: EAEU energy markets remain
functionally at stage one, incapable of absorbing the OCA-violating asymmetric shocks
[@mundell_1961] that structural energy dependency generates. The EAEU's preferential energy
pricing perpetuates Vinerian trade diversion [@viner_1950] rather than creating the
welfare-improving integration that Balassa's taxonomy requires at stage two and beyond.

The findings carry implications beyond the Eurasian case. In an era of multipolar geoeconomic
competition, energy dependency constitutes a structural constraint on sovereign economic
autonomy — a vulnerability that intensifies during periods of supply disruption and great power
rivalry. The policy agenda for energy-importing Eurasian economies must combine supply
diversification with macroeconomic buffer-building, EAEU institutional reform, and SCO
multilateral energy cooperation.

**Limitations and future research.** Several limitations warrant acknowledgment. First, the
WDI energy import dependency variable (EG.IMP.CONS.ZS) measures the share of net energy
imports in total energy use, capturing structural position but not the directional concentration
of supply sources — a country importing 80% of its energy from three diversified suppliers
occupies a different geoeconomic position than one importing 80% from a single dominant
exporter. Future research using bilateral energy trade data would allow a more precise
decomposition of supply concentration risk. Second, the sample window ends in 2022; the
post-February 2022 structural break in Eurasian energy architecture — the Russian supply
reorientation, accelerated Trans-Caspian discussions, and emergence of new LNG spot markets
— constitutes a distinct regime that may generate different coefficient estimates. Third, the
CCEMG and AMG estimators yield coefficients significant at the 10% level only; broader panel
coverage or longer time horizons would improve statistical precision. These limitations suggest
a productive agenda: a narrower EAEU panel with institutional heterogeneity variables, a
bilateral energy trade gravity model, and a Türkiye-specific ARDL analysis exploiting the full
depth of available time-series data [@imzali_bayraktutan_2025; @yalta_yalta_2017].
